title.en: Surface Integrals, the Divergence Theorem & Stokes' Theorem

body.en: This closing chapter lifts Chapter 7's Green's theorem into three dimensions, in two different directions at once: the Divergence Theorem relates a flux integral over a closed surface to a triple integral over the solid it encloses, and Stokes' Theorem relates a line integral around a curve to a surface integral over any surface it bounds. Both are genuine generalizations of Green's theorem — a fact this chapter proves directly for Stokes' theorem, rather than just asserting the family resemblance.

For a surface \( S \) with unit normal vector \( \mathbf{n} \) and a vector field \( \mathbf{F} \), the flux of \( \mathbf{F} \) through \( S \) is \[ \iint_S\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\iint_S(\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{n})\,dS — \] the surface integral of the component of \( \mathbf{F} \) perpendicular to \( S \) at each point, exactly as the line integral of Chapter 6 picked out the component of a field along a curve. Physically: if \( \mathbf{F} \) is a fluid's velocity field, flux measures the net volume of fluid crossing \( S \) per unit time.

Let \( E \) be a solid region with boundary surface \( S=\partial E \), oriented with outward-pointing normal, and let \( \mathbf{F}=(P,Q,R) \) have continuous partial derivatives on \( E \). Then \[ \iint_S\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\iiint_E\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F}\,dV,\qquad\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F}=P_x+Q_y+R_z. \]

As with Green's theorem, it suffices to prove the identity one component at a time — \( \iint_S R\mathbf{k}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\iiint_ER_z\,dV \), say — then add the analogous \( P \)- and \( Q \)-identities (proved the same way, cycling \( x,y,z \)).

Let \( E=[a,b]\times[c,d]\times[p,q] \), a box, with faces \( S_{\text{top}} \) (\( z=q \), outward normal \( \mathbf{k} \)), \( S_{\text{bot}} \) (\( z=p \), outward normal \( -\mathbf{k} \)), and four vertical side faces where \( \mathbf{k} \) is tangent to the surface, so \( R\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{n}=0 \) there and they contribute nothing. On \( S_{\text{top}} \) and \( S_{\text{bot}} \), \( dS=dx\,dy \), so: \[ \iint_SR\mathbf{k}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\iint_{[a,b]\times[c,d]}R(x,y,q)\,dx\,dy-\iint_{[a,b]\times[c,d]}R(x,y,p)\,dx\,dy=\iint_{[a,b]\times[c,d]}\big[R(x,y,q)-R(x,y,p)\big]dx\,dy. \]

By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (holding \( x,y \) fixed), \( R(x,y,q)-R(x,y,p)=\int_p^qR_z(x,y,z)\,dz \). Substituting and using Fubini (Chapter 4, Theorem 4.1) to combine the double and single integrals into one triple integral: \[ \iint_SR\mathbf{k}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\iint_{[a,b]\times[c,d]}\!\!\int_p^qR_z\,dz\,dx\,dy=\iiint_ER_z\,dV. \] Adding the \( P \)- and \( Q \)-component identities (each proved identically, integrating \( x \) or \( y \) first instead of \( z \)) gives the full theorem for a box. The general case follows by assembling any solid \( E \) from many small boxes: on shared interior faces between two adjacent boxes, the outward normals point in opposite directions, so those flux contributions cancel in pairs, leaving only the flux through \( E \)'s outer boundary \( S \) — the same telescoping idea Green's theorem uses to extend from simple regions to general ones.

label.en: Worked example 8.A — Flux via the Divergence Theorem

body.en:
Find the flux of \( \mathbf{F}=(x,y,z) \) outward through the sphere \( x^2+y^2+z^2=R^2 \).

\( \operatorname{div}\mathbf{F}=1+1+1=3 \). By the Divergence Theorem, \[ \iint_S\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\iiint_E3\,dV=3\cdot\text{Vol}(E)=3\Big(\frac43\pi R^3\Big)=4\pi R^3, \] using Chapter 5, Worked example 5.C's ball-volume formula — turning a genuinely awkward surface integral (over a curved sphere) into three times a volume already known.

Let \( S \) be an oriented surface with unit normal \( \mathbf{n} \), bounded by a positively oriented simple closed curve \( C=\partial S \) (oriented so that walking along \( C \) with your head pointing along \( \mathbf{n} \) keeps \( S \) on your left), and let \( \mathbf{F} \) have continuous partial derivatives near \( S \). Then \[ \oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\iint_S(\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S},\qquad\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F}=\nabla\times\mathbf{F}=(R_y-Q_z,\,P_z-R_x,\,Q_x-P_y). \]

label.en: Proof (Green's theorem IS Stokes' theorem for a flat region)

body.en:
Take \( S \) to be a flat region \( D \) lying in the \( xy \)-plane, with \( \mathbf{F}=(P,Q,0) \) depending only on \( x,y \) (a planar field, viewed as living in 3-space). The upward normal is \( \mathbf{n}=\mathbf{k} \), so \( dS=dA \) and \( d\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{k}\,dA \).

\[ \operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F}=(R_y-Q_z,\,P_z-R_x,\,Q_x-P_y)=(0-0,\,0-0,\,Q_x-P_y)=(0,0,Q_x-P_y), \] since \( R=0 \) and \( P,Q \) don't depend on \( z \). So \[ \iint_S(\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}=\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{k}\,dA=\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,dA, \] exactly the right-hand side of Green's theorem (Chapter 7, Theorem 7.1). And the boundary curve \( C=\partial D \), oriented so \( D \) stays on the left while walking with head along \( \mathbf{n}=\mathbf{k} \), is exactly the positively-oriented (counterclockwise) curve Green's theorem uses, with \( \oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\oint_CP\,dx+Q\,dy \) (the \( z \)-component of \( \mathbf{F} \) and \( d\mathbf{r} \) both vanish identically here). So Stokes' theorem's statement, restricted to this flat case, reduces to exactly Green's theorem — already proved in full in Chapter 7. The general case (a genuinely curved \( S \)) is proved the same way after pulling the surface integral back to a flat parameter domain via \( S \)'s parametrization — real, but more machinery than belongs here.

label.en: Worked example 8.B — Circulation via Stokes' Theorem

body.en:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate \( \oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} \) for \( \mathbf{F}=(-y,x,0) \), where \( C \) is the unit circle \( x^2+y^2=1 \) in the \( xy \)-plane, positively oriented.

\( \operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F}=(R_y-Q_z,\,P_z-R_x,\,Q_x-P_y)=(0,0,1-(-1))=(0,0,2) \).

Take \( S \) to be the flat unit disk, \( \mathbf{n}=\mathbf{k} \): \[ \oint_C\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}=\iint_S(0,0,2)\cdot\mathbf{k}\,dA=\iint_S2\,dA=2\cdot\pi(1)^2=2\pi. \]

(Direct check via Chapter 6's Definition 6.2, parametrizing \( C \) as \( (\cos t,\sin t) \): \( \int_0^{2\pi}\big[(-\sin t)(-\sin t)+(\cos t)(\cos t)\big]dt=\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi \). ✓)

value.en: Green's, Divergence & Stokes' are all \( \int_{\partial\,\text{region}}=\int_{\text{region}}(\text{derivative}) \) — the same Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, one and two dimensions up

body.en:
Use the Divergence Theorem to find the outward flux of \( \mathbf{F}=(x^2,\,y^2,\,z^2) \) through the surface of the box \( [0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1] \).

Show solution

\( \operatorname{div}\mathbf{F}=2x+2y+2z \).

\[ \iiint_E(2x+2y+2z)\,dV=\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1(2x+2y+2z)\,dz\,dy\,dx. \]

By symmetry, each of the three terms contributes the same amount: \( \int_0^1\!\int_0^1\!\int_0^12x\,dz\,dy\,dx=\int_0^12x\,dx=1 \). Total \( =1+1+1=3 \). Flux \( =3 \).

Find \( \operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F} \) for \( \mathbf{F}=(yz,\,xz,\,xy) \).

Solution: \( \operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F}=(R_y-Q_z,\,P_z-R_x,\,Q_x-P_y)=(x-x,\,y-y,\,z-z)=(0,0,0) \) — a conservative-type field in 3D (curl-free), consistent with \( \mathbf{F}=\nabla(xyz) \).

question.en: Practice: Find \( \operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} \) and \( \operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F} \) for \( \mathbf{F}=(x^2,\,-2xy,\,0) \), and state whether \( \mathbf{F} \) could be the gradient of a scalar function.

solution.en: \( \operatorname{div}\mathbf{F}=2x-2x+0=0 \). \( \operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F}=(0-0,\,0-0,\,-2y-0)=(0,0,-2y) \). Since \( \operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F}\neq\mathbf{0} \), \( \mathbf{F} \) is not conservative (a gradient field always has curl \( \mathbf{0} \), the 3D analogue of Chapter 6's \( P_y=Q_x \) test).
